claims.text: The initial single-crystal FeNiCrMn alloy has an FCC structure.
The FeNiCrMn solid solution has high lattice distortion.
Yield strength remains relatively constant from 10^-4 to 10^2 s^-1 over 77–600 K.
The dominant yielding mechanism is thermally activated dislocation nucleation.
Solute clusters or stacking-fault tetrahedra constitute the relevant nucleation obstacles.
Athermal screw-dislocation glide is not the dominant cause of yield onset.
FCC-to-BCC transformation is not the dominant cause of yield onset.
Lattice distortion creates a broad distribution of local energy barriers.
The broad barrier distribution makes thermal activation dominate yield onset throughout 77–600 K.
Thermal activation over a broad barrier distribution masks the usual strain-rate sensitivity.
Loading along a high-symmetry direction such as <111> minimizes resolved shear stress on the primary FCC slip system.
Reducing resolved shear stress by using a <111>-type loading orientation delays yield onset.
Aligning the loading axis with a high-symmetry direction minimizes crystal-orientation anisotropy effects.
Traditional FCC metals generally have strong strain-rate-sensitive yield strength because of athermal dislocation-glide mechanisms.
If FCC-to-BCC transformation is the primary deformation mode, BCC diffraction peaks should appear and grow at the yield point across all tested strain rates.
Absence of BCC peaks during yielding would falsify the claim that FCC-to-BCC transformation is the primary deformation mode.
FCC peak broadening and shifting without BCC peaks would indicate dislocation accumulation rather than phase transformation.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to polycrystals or alloys containing substantial BCC phase fractions.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis field says absence of BCC peaks would falsify the FCC-to-BCC-primary hypothesis, whereas the falsification_experiment field says falsification occurs if BCC peaks appear and grow. These statements target opposite hypotheses and therefore define incompatible falsification outcomes.
